items.title: ‘Only a part of the chest was found’: Delhi’s Nepali community tries to count the missing
items.summary: Sunita Thapa and her son Dinesh were at home in Trishuli Bazaar, in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, when the flood struck on August 26. Within moments, the family’s house and shop were gone, swallowed by the current, and so were Sunita and Dinesh. A search began, and three days later, Dinesh’s body was found in the plains of Narayangarh, badly damaged. “The body was severed. Only the upper part, above the chest, was found. The face and chest were intact, so he could be identified,” says Jeet Bahadur Ranabhat, whose wife Shobha is Sunita’s cousin. Local residents cremated Dinesh on the riverbank. Sunita remains untraced. Ranabhat’s family lives in Delhi’s Shakarpur – one of many Nepali households scattered across the city now living with a particular kind of anguish. Nepal’s floods, among the worst to hit the country in years, have already killed more than a thousand people and left thousands missing, overwhelming rescue teams and cutting off entire valleys. More than 11,000 people have been rescued from flood-affected areas in Nepal so far, while around 4,000 people were still missing. items.title: Diverting codeine cough syrup for intoxication attracts NDPS Act even if within permissible limits: Allahabad High Court
items.summary: The Allahabad High Court has ruled that possessing, transporting, or selling codeine-based cough syrup for intoxication attracts the stringent Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985, even if the codeine concentration falls within permissible limits [ Bhola Prasad v. State of U.P.]. Justice Arun Kumar Singh Deshwal held that the statutory exemption granted to codeine preparations under Entry 35 of the Central Government Notification dated November 14, 1985, is strictly conditional upon the formulation being handled for bona fide therapeutic purposes. The Court clarified that the moment such medicinal preparations are diverted to illicit supply chains for substance abuse, they lose statutory immunity and must be classified as "manufactured drugs" under Section 2(xi) of the NDPS Act. "Codeine-based cough syrup having permitted quantity of codeine, manufactured or produced as a cough suppressant, if stocked, sold or transported for other purposes (like intoxication) instead of medicinal use, would be treated as a codeine preparation under the category of Manufactured drug and would attract the provisions of the NDPS Act.
